utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, before we begin, there are some formalities that we need to do left over from yesterday. The first is to return the book, General Clark's book, which was not admitted, which we return now. There should be three copies. The next is to formally inform the parties that we are minded, subject to -- subject to any submissions, that we are minded to sit on Monday, the 26th of January, and sit that week Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. I've just had a note that the courtroom is available, but if there are any submissions from anybody, we'll hear them later in the day, but obviously we need to fix it today since it's the last day of sitting. I don't know if there are any other administrative matters to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registry also inform me that no redactions were made yesterday to the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice will have ten minutes of administrative matters to deal with at the end of the day, so nothing for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Sorry to keep you, Mr. Witness, but we're going to start now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be passed, please, his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, if you look, please, at the first page of your statement, just the front page, are the details, your personal details set out on that first page correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And, Witness, if you look, please, at the first page of the statement in English, does your signature appear on the bottom of that first page and on the last page of that statement in English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, that statement is dated the 28th of June, 1997, and are the contents of that statement true to the best of your knowledge and belief, subject to some points of clarification which we'll come to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity, is it right, since being in The Hague, to read through a copy of that statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a technical question. There is something wrong with the microphone. I can't hear anything that the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have that looked into. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, I think we need to confirm the pseudonym of the witness for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The pseudonym is B-1619 for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm hearing the interpreter, but I'm not hearing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the technical matter looked into. If you'd like to take a seat, Ms. Pack, we'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear the interpreter very well, but I cannot hear the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask to admit the statement dated 28th of June, 1997, under Rule 89(F), already the subject of a previous ruling by Your Honours on the 9th of December this year, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit the statement, and we'll ask for the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 620, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll read a short summary. The witness, a Muslim, is from Zepa in the municipality of Rogatica. He gives evidence that on the 5th of August, 1995, after the fall of Zepa, he set off with eight friends towards Priboj in Yugoslavia. At or close to the border they came across 40 men dressed in blue police camouflage uniforms. They had to surrender. These men were from Serbia. The police could -- the witness could tell this from their accents, and they wore insignia on their soldiers of the police of the Republic of Serbia. They beat the witness and his friends and then tied them two by two. They loaded them on a truck and took them in the direction of Visegrad. At the village of Klasnik in Visegrad they came across local Serbs who beat the witness and his friends. The local Serbs called Milan Lukic by radio, asking him to come. Lukic later arrived with seven or eight colleagues. The witness describes the massacre of his friends by Lukic and his men whilst they were en route from Klasnik to Visegrad. He describes his detention and interrogation in Visegrad and his subsequent detention in Rogatica prison. He saw General Mladic in Rogatica prison on four occasions. On the last occasion prior to the witness's exchange, Mladic joked at them and then his mood changed. He said, "There will be no exchange, only with Allah." Then his mood changed and he said he would let the witness be exchanged but that there would not be a second chance. On the 15th of January, 1996, a bus came, taking the witness to Kula. He was finally exchanged on the 19th of January, 1996. Your Honour, I have a couple of questions by way of clarification. Can the witness be shown his statement in B/C/S, please, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, there's a matter that you wanted to clarify in that paragraph. You say there that you went to the village of Podravanje in Srebrenica to buy food. Is it right that you went to that village yourself or did you receive food from that village, not actually going there yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No, I did not go there myself. Actually, food was brought from that village and then we bought it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, could you turn to paragraph 22, please, of the statement that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, you describe in that paragraph [French translation on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a problem with the French coming through on our channel, the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, there was a wrong gesture. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. All seems to be well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You describe in that paragraph your surrender to the police of the Republic of Serbia along with eight of your friends. Are you able to say which side of the border with Serbia, the Bosnian or the Serbian side, that you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say exactly. This happened around the border. We were surrounded from all sides, from the Serbian side and this other side, so I cannot say exactly where we surrendered. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the second tab of the exhibit bundle, the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to check whether the accused is following the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the channel that is the customary channel where the Serbian translation is, and that is also where I should hear the voice of the witness, I can hear the interpretation, but I cannot hear the witness at all. And since he is quite far away and he is speaking very softly, I cannot hear him without the microphone here in the courtroom. I don't know if Mr. Tapuskovic has the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we might try -- would the witness, if you can, come closer to the microphone. It may be that you can really come no closer than you already are, but perhaps you can, and perhaps you can speak as loudly as you can, and we'll try and resolve it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, you have in front of you a map initialed by you under your pseudonym and dated the 15th of December. Have you encircled on that map marked A the approximate area where you surrendered with your friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And within that area, do we see the town of -- the village of Stolac on the Serbian side of the border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Stolac, a mountain, a hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, that area also appears on the Prosecution Exhibit 326, page 33, reference 2E.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, going back to paragraph 22 of your statement, having tied you up two by two, you and your friends, where did the Serbian police take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: The Serbian police took us to Klasnik in the municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Whom did they leave you there with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: They handed us over there to the local Serbs, that is to say the Serbs who were probably from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did they take you or your friends to their own or any police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No. They just transferred us there. It was a kind of camp there where the local Serbs were in Klasnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, was there another group of men in Klasnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes. There were about 20 other men there too, 20 men in uniform. They were sitting apart from the rest. They were wearing the same uniforms with the same insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Were you able to tell where they were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Well, they were from Serbia, judging by their accent. They were also in uniform, and they were talking for a while. They were talking to a prisoner. So I could conclude on the basis of that conversation that they were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did you subsequently hear where specifically they were from in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that. This small unit was from Kraljevo. They explained that they knew about some particular places when they were talking to this prisoner, and the brother of one of these soldiers had some kind of a cafe or restaurant or a butcher shop in Kraljevo, and the prisoner remembered that because he did his military service before the war in the town of Kraljevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, finally, can you remember what sort uniforms these men were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: This entire group had the same camouflage uniforms. They had White Eagles' patches on their sleeves, but I did not notice their caps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've no further questions. One matter that I would like to raise before the witness is cross-examined, I've identified at the start of the summary those matters which may, if questioned upon, lead to the identification of this witness. Just two matters at the start of the summary and I'd ask Your Honour to hear those matters, if they arise, in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Not necessarily now, Your Honour, it would simply be if they arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's necessary that it be said in private session so that it can be heard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry, Mr. May, I'm not going to compromise the witness in any way. I'd never do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1619, you were underage at the time when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I can barely hear you. Let me try to put the volume up as much as possible, because it's not Ms. Pack who is speaking now. So it was only towards the end of 1995 that you became of age; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement, you say that in the month of August 1994, you were mobilised, and after basic training, you were deployed in the infantry, and after that in the rocket platoon of the anti-aircraft defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since you were mobilised as a minor, how many other minors were there who were mobilised in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. Are you referring to the entire army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't mean the entire army. I don't think that you would know what the situation was in the entire army. I'm talking about what you know, about the situation in your unit, in your area, in your group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to give a precise answer, just give me a tentative figure. How many soldiers were there? How many of you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: This brigade had about 1.200 men. Now, perhaps there were between 50 and 100 peers of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means about 10 per cent of the personnel of the brigade were children, that is to say persons who were underage, minors. Tell me, do you know that in 1993 the Security Council of the UN passed a Resolution proclaiming Zepa, in addition to other areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a demilitarised zone and a safe area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in spite of that, in the area of Zepa, there was not only a unit that was there but actually mobilisation was carried out. You were mobilised in 1994; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, you say that the war in Zepa started on the 4th of June, 1992, and in the following way, that, as you had put it, a small JNA unit came into town on -- under the pretext of delivering food to Mount Javor. That was in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then your local commander, as far as I can see from your statement because I don't have any other information related to your statement, then your local commander realised that the members of the JNA were preparing to attack, although they did not attack anyone, so then he decided to ambush them in a section of the road that was very narrow, and the sides were steep, as you say. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes. In those villages around Han Pijesak, the JNA fired from tanks and all other weapons, so this could not have been a reason why they would not go further with their armoured vehicles and men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to talk about what you heard and what you were assuming. It was my understanding that they came, they did not attack you, you simply ambushed them on the road, and both sides of the road were steep, as you had put it here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the first armed conflict was actually this ambush that you had prepared.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Well, the first biggish one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the first big armed conflict was when you, that is to say, the local unit that you had established in Zepa, placed an ambush against the JNA unit that was moving along the road. Then when that happened, you were only 14 years old. Tell me, how do you know about this? Did you participate in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I know the people who were there, and they told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this unit, your unit, the unit you're talking of, was under the command of Avdo Palic? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Not at the very beginning, but later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was the commander of that brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes. Not at first, but later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this unit was part of a larger detachment which had a different name, didn't it, Mr. 1619?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that larger unit and what was its name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: The 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really have to look at the transcript. I can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. That's the 28th Division of Naser Oric, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the fact that you are testifying, among other things, about this attack on the JNA members when, according to you, the war started in the area of Srebrenica, do you remember what occurred during that attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you hearing me well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, but could you repeat the question? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying that since you are testifying about this ambush that you -- we have just established when the war in the Zepa area started, could you tell me what actually happened during that attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I can't as I wasn't there. I already said that I wasn't a participant, so I can't describe the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You don't know the details. But is it true that in that ambush set for the JNA 45 JNA soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in addition to those 45 soldiers who were killed, another 31 are still registered as missing? Do you know where those who are still missing were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I'm not aware at all about the soldiers that went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Forty-five soldiers of the JNA were killed in that ambush, but another 31 are missing, and they were taken somewhere. You should know, as this is a small place. Where were they taken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I really am not aware of those 31 soldiers. I know nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't know anything, we can move on. In paragraph 5, you say that your men were able to repel virtually all attacks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: This paragraph relates to that day in 1992 when the JNA was heading towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the brigade that you mention was already active there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: It was just in the process of formation at the beginning of 1992, so the terrain contributed to all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You used the advantages of the terrain, the effect of surprise. You ambushed the JNA soldiers and killed 45 of them, but how strong was that unit then at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I am unable to give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear from this, Witness 1619, that it was not the Serbs who attacked you but you who attacked the JNA and killed 45 men in that first attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Before all this, maybe a month or two before it, we were blocked. Our electricity was cut off. The surrounding villages towards Rogatica had been torched. There was occasional shelling. So I think it's clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From your statement, I see you say that you were able to defend the area and apparently there was some fire in two villages only. You mention those two cases of torchings in two villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Those were villages that were on the road taken by that unit. They were going from Han Pijesak and passing those villages as they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there attacks on that unit from those villages as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: From the stories of the people who fled from there to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know, since you're claiming that, you're claiming to know that, do you know that in June, in the month of June, there were synchronised attacks by your forces on Serb villages; Agorovici [phoen], Simici, Presirici [phoen], Kozici, Pijesko [phoen], Borac, Vraselica [phoen]. These are all villages that you're familiar with, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I heard only of Presirici, and they too are close to Rogatica and that's a long way away. We had no contact with them. That's way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that when those attacks were carried out against all those villages, the people were killed, a large number of people were killed and their property looted, the villages burnt down. Even tombstones broken and destroyed and desecrated. This is a whole series of Serb villages in your immediate vicinity which these forces of yours attacked, just as they attacked this JNA column. Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I hear that for the first time from you. And after all, 40 or so kilometres is not the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That applies to this one village that you said you knew. I'm not sure whether you said one or two villages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I heard of the name of that village, but I never went there, and I hadn't heard of what you say happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that this man, the man I mentioned, Avdo Palic, that you said was later the commander, that he attacked a Serb village called Borovina, which is also in the municipality of Han Pijesak on the 7th of August, 1992, and personally killed, among other Serbs that were killed there, he personally killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How can the witness know about this? Do you know anything at all about this, Mr. 1619?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point asking him this sort of question. He Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. knows nothing about it. He said that. You can call evidence about it in due course, but it's a waste of time asking witnesses who know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can you know in advance that the witness doesn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because he's not the man you're talking about. Now, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he knew that the commander was Avdo Palic, and I'm asking him a question about the person he said he knew and he admitted that he was the commander over there, so I'm asking whether he knows about the activities of that man that he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given you an answer. He doesn't. Maybe you want to ask him about what he's given evidence about if you challenge it. General Mladic, for instance. The massacre of his friends. You may want to challenge that evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on. I'm afraid we can't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness says -- I am saying I can't get an answer to a question until I put it to him, and if the witness says that he doesn't know, then he's answered the question. He knows this man. That's why I asked him this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that these attacks on Serb villages, which went on until the spring of 1993, and in paragraph 13 you say that the inhabitants of Zepa were left without water and electricity when Zepa was blocked early in 1992. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now explain to me, please, what kind of a blockade of Zepa are you talking about at the beginning of 1992 when you yourself said that the war started on the 4th of June, which means in the middle of that year, with the ambush, your ambush of this column of soldiers that you killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I said that the first larger conflict occurred on that occasion, but you're well aware when Serb autonomous regions started to be formed at the beginning of 1992. I already said that all approaches, all telephone lines, power supplies, and everything else was blocked, and refugees started coming in from Rogatica and Visegrad at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And how long were you without electricity, water, telephone lines, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: From 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From when in 1992? You say at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I'm really not able to give you an exact date, but it was the very beginning of the year, the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. But at the beginning of 1992, there was absolutely no conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying do you -- are you aware that at the beginning of 1992 there were absolutely no conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as I know, there were sporadic clashes, I think in Bijeljina what happened happened, and around Zepa there were sporadic clashes and refugees from coming from Visegrad and Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. There's no need to speak about dates then, because -- well, after all, you don't even have to know these things. Anyway, tell me, please, certainly you do know that in addition to Zepa, the neighbouring town of Srebrenica was proclaimed a demilitarised safe area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16, you say that in June 1995, you returned from Srebrenica to Zepa where you had attended additional military training; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in Srebrenica, the command and the bulk of the units of the 28th Division were stationed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is where the training centre was as well, the one you went to. How long did you attend training there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I think for about 15 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of additional training was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I think you can see that from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sabotage reconnaissance. What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No, no, it isn't that. It is training for anti-air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So throughout that time since you were undergoing training and that was where the 28th Division was based, your brigade in Zepa, the centre in Srebrenica, throughout that time, units of the 28th Division were in that demilitarised zone of Srebrenica and Zepa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Well, the boundaries of the demilitarised zone were smaller than the actual territory, which was - I don't know how to call it - in between the zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that those units of the 28th Division, which means your division, completely razed to the ground all the surrounding Serb villages and killed the entire Serb population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was supposed to carry out the demilitarisation and the disarming of your forces? Was it the UN members who were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 18, you say that in July 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, Zepa was attacked, and UNPROFOR at the time, as you say, did nothing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain, please, how could it have done anything when you yourself in that same paragraph say that at three checkpoints of theirs you seized their weapons and chased them to their base? Is that right, Mr. 1619?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Because when the attack on Zepa started, during the first couple of days they went to their shelters, and those who were at the checkpoint, they didn't do anything, even to report what was happening. So we came to the conclusion that they wouldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you seized their weapons from them, you disarmed the UNPROFOR officers and chased them back to their base.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: We didn't chase them there. Their officer was there, and together with all the things they wanted to take with them, their personal belongings, they were driven to their base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you escorted them back to their base. This is what you say in your statement, and I'm quoting you. So it is a polite way of saying that you disarmed them and took them to their base.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, but we didn't chase them off, we didn't drive them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, you escorted them to their base. But actually, you snatched away their weapons, you didn't just take them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: The officer who was there, in agreement with our commander, they agreed amongst themselves that they -- he, too, should go and that the weapons should be taken away. There was no force used, no coercion. They just wanted to reach their main base and probably wait for the outcome of all those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true that the fighting around Zepa went on for all of ten days and that they were stopped when General Smith arrived, who then brought some order, agreement was reached for the wounded and the civilians to be taken out of Zepa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that it was only members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who remained in Zepa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, on the mountains above Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So everybody left except for the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In paragraph 20, you say that Avdo Palic, your local brigade commander, surrendered on that occasion to the members of the army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: It wasn't only members of the army who had stayed back. There were also a number of civilians in the mountains, men who did not dare join these convoys and these trucks. They were afraid. A number of them stayed back together with the army. And as concerns what I said about the commander, I can explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead and explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: When the last few buses left Zepa, on Mount Boksanica, that is to say on the road towards Rogatica, then the Serbs stopped these civilians. So it is true that they got out of Zepa, but they were stopped at Boksanica. And as I wrote in my statement - you can check that - then he surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did this number of men that you refer to stay back? Why didn't they dare leave with the other civilians? Why didn't they join the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Because they were afraid that they would be taken off the buses, as indeed happened with about 50 or so men who I found later in prison. They were taking wounded persons off buses and also older men, about 50 years old, who were suspected of having been members of the army. So they got them off the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But is it correct, Mr. 1619, that Avdo Palic did not surrender? He was taken prisoner, rather, in this fighting with members of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the problem now? Now he has a problem? Microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First and foremost, he did not surrender during the fighting, because a cease-fire had been signed during those days and he was down there involved in the negotiations together with members of UNPROFOR, and the Serbs quite simply took him out of the UNPROFOR base in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No, but his escort was allowed to return to the Zepa mountains, and he's the one who told us what happened, because they sent him so that he'd talk everybody else into surrendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, they kept this Palic and they sent his escort back to the unit to inform the unit that everybody should surrender; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now you've clarified this for me. Tell me, you conveyed something to the deputy commander. This has to do with paragraph 20. You heard that one of members of the Ukrainian Battalion asked to speak to Palic, that he had been killed while attempting to flee, and you said that to the deputy commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes. I heard this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of Palic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Major Ramo Cardakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he one of the persons who were later in the woods in this group together with you? I'm not going to refer to any names in order to protect your identity. What happened to him? What happened to this deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I don't know what happened. Later on, there was general disarray up there, so I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there is no doubt that this message that came that this unit should surrender was not accepted and that the unit went on fighting; is that right? Even after Palic was taken prisoner, the unit went on fighting, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, but people were waiting up there to hear what the outcome of the negotiations would be. So during the cease-fire, we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's see now. Your father, who was also in the ranks of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, decided with the rest to go to Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: It's not true that he was a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That he decided to go to Serbia and surrender, that is correct, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you did not want to go with him. You wanted to stay there and indeed you did stay there with another eight friends and you withdrew into the forest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did your father go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. He did not go by himself. Did he go with a considerable number of other people to Serbia too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. A couple of hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A couple of hundred. When you say "a couple of hundred" in Serbian, that means several hundred. It does not mean a couple as literally 200. Tell me, when did you meet up with your father again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: The first time after that was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Where was he during all this time after having gone to Serbia and until 1999 when you met up with him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: In the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, did he tell you how he was treated in Serbia; that he was treated decently, politely, that nobody mistreated him? Did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Well, that was his own case, yes, but there were other cases too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As for him himself, and he was probably not the only one, he was treated decently, properly, and there was no mistreatment involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, but he was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean he was staying at some centre, and after that he was sent where he wanted to go and then he went to America; right? Is that right, Mr. 1619?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: He did go to America, but he told me that this was decided by the Red Cross and the UNHCR. So they didn't have much choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The UNHCR said where people could go depending on the receiving country, how many they were willing to take in, but it was his choice to leave Serbia, and nobody prevented him from leaving Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, whether he was allowed to go to Australia or America or Germany, that was not up to the Serbian authorities, as you know full well. Tell me, please, you say in paragraph 21 -- I'm not going to mention all these names so we don't have to move into private session. I bear in mind the fact that this is a paragraph that should not be read out. So with a group of fellow combatants, you remained where you were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, since -- since you have here one of these comrades of yours, this is the first one you mention in paragraph 21 -- let me check once again. Here it is. It's the end of paragraph 21 when you say this number of people, I'm not even going to say how many people were there, were, and now you mention the names. And the first name that is written here, the first name so that we don't have to move into private session, do you know that this person, on the 28th of August, 1992, in the village of Okruglo, near Rogatica, intercepted a passenger car in which Radenko Djelakovic [phoen] was as well as his daughter Sonija? So this was a man who was travelling with his daughter. And this person mentioned here killed both of them; do you know that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No, because I've already said, as for all these things that happened around Rogatica, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spent a long time together. It was not a big group. You did not hear from him about all the things he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: First of all, it wasn't that we spent a long time together. We were together perhaps for three or four days, and this group was formed simply by chance up there in the mountains during this general disarray, as I said. So people simply stayed with the first person they came across. So I really don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fourth person on this list after the brackets that we see here in the text, do you know that in 1992 in the village of Stitarevo he also committed a murder? The murdered man was called Nedzo Lindevic, from Trsevina. And he also seriously wounded another man. I'm just asking about people who were in your group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I'm telling you yet again we were in that group together by chance. I do not know what happened in other towns. This man is from a different place altogether, so I'm telling you yet again that this group was simply formed by chance at that time, and we really didn't have all that time to get acquainted and to talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In any event, even if it were true, these allegations, what's the relevance of it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant, Mr. May, so that you would understand the situation in the area, in the area all the way to Bratunac. If you look at the map, you will see this easily. All the Serb villages were destroyed by Naser Oric's 28th Division. Everything was torched, everybody was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all defence. And is it in any way suggested that that in some way justified these men being killed, as this witness has set out in his statement? Is that what's being suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course it's not justified by that. Heaven forbid. A crime cannot justify another crime. I am talking about a situation in which you see that this conflict started. It started by an ambush aimed against a JNA column. An enormous number of soldiers were killed, 45 of them, ambushed. After that, they torched everything all around them, and that's how the conflict broke out. And now whether people were taken prisoner were killed, of course nobody can justify that. That's a shame.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you now because you just said that this group was set up by chance to such an extent that you quite literally didn't know anybody from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I knew two men a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These two men you knew a bit better, were you aware of the activities of the two in respect of the matters we were discussing just now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Well, one of them was even younger than I was, as a matter of fact, and the other one was my age, and all the rest were older men. So of course I was more or less together with these two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were all together in one brigade, one unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I have to ask you about a relative of yours, so that would probably identify you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. May, could we just move into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you about your crossing in 1992. You crossed the Drina on the 5th of August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misspoke. In 1995, yes. So you crossed the Drina on the 5th of August, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: On the night of the 4th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where exactly did you cross the Drina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: As I was there only once in my whole life, that is on that occasion, I am not quite sure, but I think it's called Brusnicki Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, this canyon, this spot where we crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you cross the Drina using a bridge or did you swim over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: We built a raft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you crossed to the other bank of the Drina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes. And Serbia is on the other bank and not Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Not throughout. Not everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the other bank of the Drina, across the way from the place you mentioned, you say you were arrested by the police of the Republic of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I already said that somewhere around the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the point. You crossed the Drina, and then on the other side of the Drina, where Serbia is, it is only natural that the police of the Republic of Serbia should guard its border on its bank. So you crossed the Drina illegally. As you say, you crossed in a raft, several of you, and then the police turned you back to the other bank, to the other side, because they didn't receive you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: That they turned us back, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when they took you back, they crossed the Drina again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I'm repeating: They didn't go back across the Drina. And also, where we crossed the Drina, it wasn't Serbia. You would have to walk for half a day to reach the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 1619, let us not go into that now, but in any event, the police, which you say was the police of the Republic of Serbia, arrested you on the other side of the Drina, which you had crossed illegally, and then they took you back and that's all. Tell me, they handed you over to the authorities on your own territory, is that right, after you had illegally entered Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, they took us to Klasnik and handed us over to the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me find the place in the statement. I saw somewhere, and I'm unable to find it now, but I saw that you said that they took you to their police station. They didn't take you to their police station, they took you back; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: They took us back to Klasnik, to a camp, a base or whatever, of the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that's the closest location where any local authorities were to be found. And those men who took you back, did they go back to Serbia after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: They left there. Where they went to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They stopped you, they took you back, and then they left; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So those men that you saw who were policemen from Serbia, they didn't beat you or mistreat you in any way? They didn't inflict any injuries, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No, that's not right. They did mistreat us. They made us strip to our waist, they collected everything we had on us - money and jewellery and everything else - and only then did they take us down there to Klasnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If these were policemen on the Serbian side, I find it difficult to believe that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: That's your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you say of them that they had White Eagles patches on their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No. I said that regarding another group of soldiers who were in Klasnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milosevic. If I can clarify this. Of course you may not answer, but Mr. Milosevic, do you agree, accept that these policemen are Serbian police who caught this group of people? I notice on the map, even if they crossed the river, it's not the border. So you accept that Serbian police are inside Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not accept that the police of the Republic of Serbia was in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Kwon. I am sure that the police of the Republic of Serbia could only have been on the territory of the Republic of Serbia. That is why if you cross the Drina, you enter Serbia on this side, and they could have been arrested by the police of Republic of Serbia only in the Republic of Serbia. And even if -- so I'm answering your question though you don't insist I do so: Even in that case, if the police of the Republic of Serbia had been there, they would have taken them to their own police station, identified them, and treated them then accordingly, either as refugees or some kind of misplaced -- displaced persons. So regarding your question whether the police of the Republic of Serbia was on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, my answer is no, they weren't, nor could they be, nor would we have risked the lives of our men to cross to the other side where a war was being waged. There was only a single platoon of our police on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina about which I notified Owen and Stoltenberg in the Strpce station where a train was stopped and people taken off it. This is the Belgrade-Bar railway line, going from Belgrade to Bar, and for nine kilometres it runs through the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Only for nine kilometres. And on that stretch, there is a small station called Strpce where the train never stops. However the train was stopped there, people taken off the train and killed. And this was done by some paramilitaries, and then we sent a police platoon there to secure the station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We've heard that. You can go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, because this was an exception, this is an exception that I informed Owen and Stoltenberg about, that we were securing our own train that was passing through that territory for a stretch of nine kilometres to protect it against paramilitaries of Republika Srpska, not Muslim units. They were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, please -- I leave something out because I see my time is running out. I was confused by what you said, that they took you to their police station. So that would mean that they took you to a Serbian police station if you were in Serbia, but they didn't take you to their police station if they were policemen from Serbia. They could have been Serbian policemen only on the territory of Serbia. So you were taken to the authorities on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, as one of the Serbs told you, they called Milan Lukic, who arrived shortly after that and shook hands with all of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this prompted you to think that the rumours about him were not true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is he from that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I think he is from the municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that seven men were killed from your group there and that Milan Lukic brought their uniforms and boots; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The numbers don't quite coincide because it would now appear that there were more of you, but that is not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's clarify to make it clear. How many men did you start off with, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Myself and another eight.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my understanding was, on the basis of what you said before, that you were eight in all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Myself plus eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then this last one was killed, as you say, this -- the eighth one then. Let me not mention the names for your own protection that you have been granted. And you alone were allowed to live; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why, if all the others were killed, why you were left alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who killed these men, and why did he take their boots and uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: You would have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the people with Milan Lukic, you say that there was another man with the same surname; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a relative of his?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that man from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 26, will you please clarify this for me. You say that a policeman in Visegrad asked you whether you knew who had brought you there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who brought you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you say you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I was scared. I was afraid of saying anything and of revealing knowing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told him you didn't know, and then he explained to you that no one would hurt you. When did you actually learn, or, rather, when did you identify that person as being Milan Lukic; when he captured you or when? When did you identify him? Was it in Visegrad or before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: He didn't capture us. When he arrived, he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, I see. That's clear. He came and he introduced himself. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got two minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will hurry up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mention a certain Zoran Neskovic. You say that he was the prison warden, then a Vujic, who took you to the prison in Rogatica. Were they also locals from the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, from Rogatica. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this Kusic you mention too, he is a man from the area, too, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in uniform, those of you who were in prison then, in that prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Which prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the Rogatica prison, or generally when you were captured, were you wearing uniforms of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Not all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this young man who was younger than you, he was wearing a uniform too, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the third person mentioned, was he also a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain, please: You say that in the cell in the Rogatica prison, a drunk came in, a drunken man came in and said he was General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes. I know it was him because I had seen him before on television, so I know it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 35, you say that Mladic visited you another three times, on the 17th of November, the 18th of December, on the 11th of January, and that he was always drunk. Is it really possible that the commander of the army of Republika Srpska should come to visit you in Rogatica several times and that throughout he was drunk? It sounds improbable to me, so could you please explain on what grounds you came to the conclusion that it was indeed General Mladic? What was he looking for, coming to see you in the cell? Why did he come? Could you explain that? It's unbelievable. It simply sounds unbelievable, so I'd like you to explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: First of all, we weren't friends for him to come and visit me personally. Each time he came, the commander, Rogatica commander, was always with him and they behaved as friends. And each time he toured the prison or camp, every time TV cameras were with him. Now, why he entered my cell each time, I really don't know, you'd have to ask him. But he didn't come to see me personally, he was just touring the facilities and he came into the cell. And it wasn't hard to see that he was drunk by the smell, the odour and his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That's two minutes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a moment ago you said that you knew Mladic because you'd seen him many times on television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Television, the papers, et cetera, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm going back to this just to clarify one matter, because here in paragraph 34 - will you look, please, at the Serbian version - you said: "On the 31st of August, we heard a lot of noise," and then you say, "Then a man came in whom I didn't know and who was drunk, and he introduced himself as General Mladic." So your explanation in the statement is different. You said that somebody who came in was a person you didn't know. So could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: When he talked in, I didn't. I didn't immediately recognise him. But only when he started talking -- whenever somebody walked in, I had to look down, I had to bow my head. I didn't dare look anyone in their eyes, in their face. But when he started speaking, I immediately realised who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at paragraphs 4 and 5, please. You talk about the first clashes, and you mention the date of 4th of April, 1992, and in paragraph 5 you say that you were able to repel Serb attacks. And then you say that after those conflicts, bodies were exchanged. Were there casualties on both sides as early as that, and then bodies of the victims being exchanged? Could you explain to the Judges how many people were killed and how many bodies would be exchanged on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: The first case, as you can see, was when those bodies that were killed in 1992, there was a bus full of women and children that the Serbs were holding captive. Those were from Rogatica, the women and children, not from Zepa. And then that busload of women and children were exchanged for the bodies. They had no family or anyone. And then those were the bodies that our men were able to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whose bodies were they? Were they bodies of Muslim victims or both sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: The bodies of Serb soldiers were exchanged, were given to the Serb side, and in return they gave us a bus full of women and children that were held captive in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few more points of clarification for Their Honours linked to paragraphs 16 and 17. In Srebrenica, in Zepa, you were during these critical events in June and July; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I was in Srebrenica, as I said already, for 15 days - I don't want to repeat myself - and also prior to these last events when it was relatively peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you were in Zepa when all these things were happening in July. You were both in Srebrenica and in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this unit that you belonged to, you said a moment ago, numbered 1.500 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Maybe less, about 1.200.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the members of that military unit, were they all armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how many were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I'm really unable to say because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then what did the people who were unarmed do? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: What weapons there were were used on the front lines, and people would take shifts, and they didn't have any particular activities, those who stayed down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in paragraph 16, in the middle of that paragraph, you say: "I had normal duties, and my position was on the front lines in front of the UN positions." Does that mean that even on the front lines, in direct contact with representatives of the UN, there were people without weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, will you look what you say in paragraph 16. "I had normal duties, manning a position on the front lines in front of the UN positions." In those positions on the front lines, were there people without weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I am unable to give you a very precise answer to that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was happening on the front lines? Were there conflicts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, did your units go outside the boundaries of the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Only if they went on foot, if people were travelling to Srebrenica and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me just this, please, if you can explain to the Judges regarding those events: How many victims were there among your fighters, among your combatants during those ten days of fighting, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure, because there was general chaos afterwards, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you can't tell us exactly how many men from your unit, your friends, your co-combatants were killed out of the 1.500 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I'd really rather not make any assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there victims? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple of short questions. Could the map in fact be put on the ELMO. And if the witness could be passed a pen. A pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, if you're able to, could you identify on the map that's been put on the ELMO just to the left of you, could you identify on that map, marked with an X, where it was approximately that you crossed the Drina. If you're not able to help, then please say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you were asked questions about your father and about his time in Serbia. He was kept there for some months, you said, before going to the United States. Do you know where he was kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was some camp in the village of Sljivovica. I don't know exactly where this is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If the witness can mark the place where his father had crossed the Drina River before. Can you locate it on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because perhaps five or six days before that, we had already parted. So I didn't know anything. I didn't even know whether he was alive or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And just finally, was he free to leave the location at which he was kept or was he kept there as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1619
utterances.text: He was a prisoner. He could not leave whenever he wanted to. Even his mail was censored, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want that marked map, Ms. Pack, to be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, I would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That can be added as a tab to Exhibit 620, tab --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 3. Thank you. Witness B-1619, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. You will just have to wait until the blinds are drawn before you do go. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could briefly go into private session for a protective measure issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could be shown a piece of paper with your name on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's, Your Honours, the last exhibit, tab 11 of his package.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you please confirm that this is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: Could the witness please be asked to speak louder and to come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked if you would, so the interpreters could hear, if you would come closer to the microphone and speak up so that we can hear. Yes. We haven't yet got an exhibit number, I think, for this package. It may be convenient to deal with that now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 621.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm not sure whether the transcript has captured that you have confirmed that this was your name. Can you please do it again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Now, did you testify in the Krstic trial on 13 April 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would like to suggest that this package be admitted under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And with your permission, I'd like to read out a brief summary of the testimony of this witness. This witness is a Bosnian Muslim who was only 17 years old when the Srebrenica enclave fell. Although many of Srebrenica's Muslims sought refuge at the UN base in Potocari, the witness fled into the woods because he feared for his life. The witness joined a column of 1 to 2.000 mostly unarmed Muslim men who tried to escape through the woods towards Tuzla and eventually surrendered along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. He was then taken to a meadow near Sandici where approximately 1.000 to 2.000 captured Muslim men gathered. They were guarded by soldiers, and one of them told the detained men that the soldiers were from Serbia. Shortly thereafter, another group of soldiers arrived and made the men clap their hands and sing "Long live the King, long live Serbia." Several hours later, the witness and the other men were taken on extremely overcrowded buses to Bratunac where they were forced to spend the night still packed onto these trucks with no food and very little water. The next day, on July 14, 1995, in the morning, the trucks continued to Zvornik and finally stopped at a location called Petkovci. Around 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon, the men were taken into a school building and crammed into classrooms under conditions perhaps even worse than on the trucks. Once inside, soldiers forced the men to say, "This is Serb land, always was and always will be." They also shouted that Srebrenica had always been and always would be Serb. The Muslim detainees were so thirsty that they began to drink their own urine. As night fell, prisoners from other classrooms were taken out in groups of three to five and shots were heard in front of the school. Eventually, soldiers began leading the Muslim prisoners out of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. school, tying their hands and loading them on a big truck. As the witness left the school, he felt a sticky substance under his feet and saw a big pile of what he thought were killed prisoners from the school. The truck onto which the witness was loaded travelled for about five to ten minutes. After it stopped, men were taken off the truck in groups of five, and each time shots were heard. The men remaining on the bus tried to avoid getting off, knowing that they would be executed. Some people shouted, "Give us some water first and then kill us." And the witness felt sorry that he would die thirsty and was trying -- and tried to hide amongst the people as long as he could, like everybody else. He just wanted to live another second or two. When the witness was eventually removed from the bus, from the truck, he was told to find a place by the Serb soldiers, and then he saw rows and rows of dead bodies. The witness and the other men reached an empty spot and were ordered by the soldiers to lie down. As the men tried to lie down, the soldiers opened fire. The witness was shot in the right side of his chest and lay suffering as the soldiers continued to line up and shoot prisoners for what the witness estimates to be anywhere from ten minutes to an hour. As the witness lay bleeding, another group of prisoners was executed next to him, and he was hit once again in his left foot, and later he received another shot. Once the shooting stopped, the witness heard the soldiers laughing and mocking the dead Muslims. Then he heard someone ordering a soldier to inspect the bodies to make sure no one had survived. The witness lay silently as a military boot stepped next to his face and then watched as the soldier fired a shot into the head of the man lying next to him. After the soldiers left, the witness escaped with another man who was wounded in the head. The two men helped each other with their teeth to untie their hands and climbed through the forest up to a hill to a spot that give them a view of the Petkovci dam area.
