The next morning, from their vantage point on the hill, they saw a yellow loader collecting dead bodies and loading them onto a tractor or a truck. The witness saw a very large pile of bodies. After four days walking through the woods, the witness and his companion finally reached Muslim territory and safety. With your permission, Your Honours, I would like to ask the witness just a very few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we heard that you escaped with your companion. Can you tell the Court how important this companion was for you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Actually, I never would have even tried to run away. I was just waiting to die. I was suffering so badly. I was thinking of calling them to shoot me. Actually, I would have been grateful to them had they killed me, I was suffering so badly. So if it hadn't been for this man, I never would have even tried to do this. He's the only one who knows how badly I suffered. Actually, I couldn't even walk. So then he'd leave me behind and then come back and beseech me to go on, but it was so hard for me to go on, it hurt so badly. When that military boot stopped right by me, I thought, They're going to kill me now, and I wanted to be killed then because I really couldn't take it any longer. But I didn't dare call out to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we also heard that you were wounded a second time and a third time. Can you describe to Their Honours how that occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, you said that it was a bus but it was actually trucks that we were on. So shooting was heard, and it was quite clear to everyone that this was the end. So people didn't want to get off. Serb soldiers were yelling, saying that we had to get off or otherwise they'd come and get us. We were all hiding behind each other. So I had to get off too. When I came there, they told us to choose our place. I didn't know what place they meant. And as I got closer, I saw that there were rows of corpses there. Everything happened so fast. And I thought I'd die soon, I wouldn't suffer. And I thought my mama will never know where I am. And some of the soldiers said that we'd fall then and then the firing started. I just know that I was hit on the right side, in the right arm. I really cannot remember the moment when I was actually hit. I felt the stench of gunpowder. There were bullets flying all around me, hitting other people, and I was just waiting for the next one to hit me. When the next row was hit, then a bullet hit me in the foot. That hurt the worst. I wish I could have screamed, but I didn't dare to. The man next to me was moaning so badly as he was dying, that he was heard a great deal. That's why perhaps the soldier didn't hear me. He came and he simply shot the man next to me in the head. So when he -- they probably used tracer bullets. I still have -- fragmentation bullets, actually, and two of them grazed me on the neck, and I was wondering, My goodness, why don't I just die?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, let me briefly ask you about your father. Was he with you when you left the enclave towards the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: He was with me at first, but later on we got lost. I lost him, actually. I was holding onto him. So when all of this commotion started and this chaos, I got lost. I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was your uncle with you at that time as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, I found him later. Actually, I found him several times and lost him several times. Later on, I found him, and he was probably killed too. His daughter was only a year old then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And a final question: We heard that you didn't want to go to the UN base in Potocari because you feared for your life. Can you explain to the Judges what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, actually when the attack on Srebrenica started, and actually even before that, it became obvious that UNPROFOR could not protect us. Actually, they were dancing to the tune of the Serbs, something like that. I was close to the line, close to the UNPROFOR points, and I saw that as soon as the Serbs started shooting, UNPROFOR would leave, even before the refugees started pouring in. So I decided not to go to UNPROFOR. Perhaps my chance of surviving was greater if I went through the woods, and perhaps more people survived among those who went through the woods. Two relatives of mine, or, rather, quite a few of them, but the two I saw right there when we parted, they went to the military base. Both of them were killed, and one was exhumed a year ago. Many of my relatives -- actually, none of my close relatives really survived. All of them were killed regardless of whether they went through the woods or to the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question is: Are you surprised to what has happened to you and your colleagues in July 1995, having lived in the Srebrenica enclave for a while as a refugee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: In actual fact, I wasn't surprised. It's the same thing that awaited us in 1992, but we managed to flee. In 1992, also in the beginning of May, the Serb army torched our house, and we escaped thanks to our neighbour. However, it was the same fate that awaited us there, like in Vlasenica and elsewhere. So it was just this killing of ours that was postponed. Perhaps I would have not lost my life myself, but most Muslims were killed, and my father was killed too. And I'm not saying this just like that. I'm saying it on the basis of what happened to my neighbours who decided to stay on, who did not want to flee. They were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could give the year of his birth, in open session or in private session, either. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I would prefer private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell Judge Kwon the exact birth date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: 15th of April, 1978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1401, you gave a few statements about the events that you're testifying about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You gave the first statement on the 19th of July, 1995, to the command of the 246th Mountain Brigade, to the security organ of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you gave your second statement to the state security service in Tuzla of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 31st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Finally, you gave a statement to the investigators, first on the 12th and 13th of August, 1995, and then on the 19th of August, 1996, and brief notes on the 4th of January and the 1st of September, 1999. But in order to handle this better, perhaps we can call the statement to the investigators the third statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, I know approximately all the statements that I gave. And then when you show me the statement, then I can tell you, well, yes, that's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that they are yours because I received them from the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, then they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think so because they bear their numbers as well. In the beginning of the month of July 1995 when the conflict broke out in Srebrenica, you were a minor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until then, with your parents and your sisters, you lived at Slapovci, a refugee centre near Tuzla, seven or eight kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Slapovici is the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please correct me if I make a mistake because I am not familiar with these localities so mistakes are possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With your family, when the conflict broke out, you went towards Suceska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you stayed in the village of Viogor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where there were a large number of people from Srebrenica and the surrounding area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this third statement, I am referring to the statement given to the investigators --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- in August 1995, in paragraph 2 you've said that your father said to you then that you should decide for yourself whether you want to go with the column of women and children to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari or to stay with the other military-aged men and try to reach the liberated territory. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, in your first statement, given on the 19th of July, 1995, as well as your second statement, of the 31st of July, 1995, you stated that then somebody issued an order that all military-aged men and able-bodied men go to Jaglici and Susnjari and further on to Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Could you just repeat what you said just now, this last sentence, what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to establish the following: A few minutes ago, you confirmed to me what it says in the statement given to the investigators, that your father said to you that you should decide for yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the first statement, of the 19th of July, and the second statement, of the 31st of July, you say, and now I'm quoting you, that: "Somebody then issued an order for all military men capable of serving in the military to set off towards Jaglici and Susnjari and then carry on towards Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I don't understand. What's in dispute? I mean, what are you trying to ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to establish whether, as you said in the statement to the investigators, whether you decided on your own because your father told you to decide on your own and then you went where you went in accordance with your own decision or was this based on an order that was issued, which is on the first page of your first statement, somewhere around the middle of the page. Somebody -- someone issued the order for all men of serving -- capable in serving in the military or, rather, all men to set out towards Jaglici and Susnjari and then to carry on towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I'll explain. I think -- it's not that I strictly said that somebody issued an order. Actually, we heard that someone had issued an order, or, rather, that someone had said that all military-age able-bodied men should go, or that would be a good thing, something like that. And what my father said to me, that has nothing to do with these orders. He said that I could decide for myself. Everybody could decide for themselves whether they would go there, to Potocari, or somewhere else. So we heard that an order had been issued but it wasn't a strict order. Everybody decided for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to hurt you in any way in view of what you've been through, but I just want to establish what actually happened. So I'm just asking you about the facts and what you said. And also, you say in your own statement: "In Viogor, after one day, my mother and three sisters went towards Potocari, hoping that they would find protection in the UNPROFOR camp, and I, together with my army, went on orders from the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's what it says quite literally. "Together with all other able-bodied men I went to Susnjari. At Susnjari there was a line-up of about 15.000 men." Is that what you stated in this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: All the details are not covered in the statement. Two or three pages are not sufficient for me to say everything. And depending on what the investigators asked me, I answered, so I may not have remembered all the details. You can have a look when I gave the statement, as soon as I crossed into that territory. Maybe I didn't remember all the details. We had heard that somebody had issued the orders. Probably the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Not the Serbs, surely. Who else could have given such an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this second statement of yours which you gave to the state security service in Tuzla on the 31st of July, you say that upon orders of the army command together with the others, you enter Susnjari and you lined up together with the other 15.000 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: All these statements are correct. All you're saying is correct, only some statements have more details, another one has less details, but it is all true. We heard it. I didn't receive a piece of document, a piece of paper with the order on it or a document, but we heard that the command had issued such an order and that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then there was a lineup. You were lined up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: It didn't go as smoothly as it is stated in the statement. There Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were a large number of civilians there. You're trying to say that these were soldiers, but it wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not trying to say anything, I'm just trying to establish the truth. So there was a line-up, and there were some 15.000 of you lining up there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Actually, I and the civilians and many others had decided to go there, and it was only later on, after the line-up, that the civilians were the last. So the army didn't really let us go. Maybe all the details are not given there. The army told us to stay last. That is what I heard, at least. There were crowds there. There was shelling. There was general confusion. I even got lost. I lost my father, then I'd find him again, because I was trying to move on together with the army, but the soldiers would chase us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but let's clear up one point. A witness testified before you from the same area who was mobilised to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who was also underage. Were you a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I would have been happy to be one, and if I had a weapon, this probably wouldn't have happened in this way. I may have got killed in the woods somewhere, but not like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you just joined this military column; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many civilians were there attached to that military column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: It's difficult to estimate. There were many people, but there were far more civilians than soldiers. I could see by the weapons, whether they were carrying a weapon or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was your father at the time a member of the 284th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I'll have to explain that. Actually, my father was a member of the brigade until Srebrenica was demilitarised. When it was demilitarised, he was no longer a soldier. He may have formally been a soldier on paper, but he didn't have a weapon. Throughout the period of conflict, when the attack on Srebrenica started, he was with us, with us children and my mother. He never went to the front line. So that's the kind of soldier he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was his commander? Who was in command of the 284th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know which brigade it is. I just recalled and I said it. I remember him saying that he was in that brigade, but I can't remember who was the commander and where the brigade was, because the area was demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but as far as I know, even though it was a safe area and proclaimed to be demilitarised, Naser Oric's 28th Division was there in Srebrenica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, maybe. I can't talk about that at any length, but I'll tell you as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that. I didn't see the army acting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Can I just add something? This 28th Division, after the demilitarisation, may have been there only formally, because they were condemned to failure anyway even before that. And when the weapons were taken away, I think they really existed only in form and not in reality, not a unit that could have done any harm to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, this column that was lined up and set off, its aim was to break its way through to Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement as well as in your second statement, you say that that column, close to the village of Kamenica, was ambushed by Serb forces, as you say; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say this in both your first and second statement, that close to the village of Kamenica the column was ambushed by Serb forces, as you say; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. There aren't enough details there, but I'll explain everything. Everything is right, but let me just add something. The column wasn't moving smoothly. The shelling had started much earlier on, and there were many killed, and there were many people who went mad. So it wasn't ambushed all at once. This happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that, "The column was broken up and divided into two and that a large number of people were killed there or seriously wounded and that there was widespread panic so that I, too, was separated from my father and I only had my Uncle Dzemal next to me." So there was a conflict there. The place is called Siljkovici. In brackets it says Kamenica. I'm just reading from your statement. And that is where the column was divided up. There were many casualties, many people dead and many wounded and widespread panic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Let me just add, the statement is an abbreviated version of things, but let me explain. The column went quietly for a short time. After that, it was constantly exposed to shelling. The column continued. They picked up the wounded as they could, and then the real shelling became so heavy that it was not possible to move forward. And I assume the column was broken off, I couldn't see it from the air or anything, I wasn't in a plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is when the fighting started between the Serb forces and your forces, is that right, in that column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: We could hear the shooting in front of us all the time, and there were shells falling around us. There were many dead people. There was a conflict in front of us. And as I reached the spot, I saw that there were a large number of people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the battle that took place before you reached it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes. We reached there afterwards, once the army had passed, so we stayed behind there. So I remember when a man wanted to join the soldier, the soldier wouldn't let them. They would chase them away. "You can't do that," they would say. But there were many people wounded. There were a lot of us, and they wouldn't let us go with them because the army couldn't pass either because there were many people wounded. There was a lot of yelling and shouting and screaming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the army broke through and left you behind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: They tried to save themselves. Otherwise, if they had taken all of us with them, I don't think anyone would have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in this breakthrough, there were a large number of dead; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, when I reached that spot, I saw many dead people. But even before, there were many bodies left behind in the woods because no one could help them. This hurt me. I -- this moved me. There was a young man crying and begging not to be left behind, but he couldn't be picked up. People were just trying to save their lives because there were shells falling all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. So actually, the greatest part of the military column broke through. Some were killed. Those who were not killed or wounded managed to break through, and they left you behind; is that right? They couldn't take you with them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: There were far more wounded, I would say, than dead. A part of the army, maybe the first part, was cut off. So maybe a part of the army clashed with the Serbs. They were broken up. But the largest part may have reached close to free territory, and they had to fight their way through. You know, 15.000 men going one behind another makes an enormous column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But the part closer to the front line managed to break through, and the part that was further away from the front line didn't manage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Let me just say the column was moving. The soldiers were up in front. I assume so. Maybe there have been one, two, 3.000 men with weapons, and they were up front. And when the column was broken into two, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. most of them stayed behind. Some of them broke through, then were killed. Those were soldiers, but others were civilians. Maybe one or two were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There must have been more than 3.000 soldiers, as you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I didn't say 3.000. I said one, two, 3.000. But I don't believe that there were more. Maybe on paper there may have been many soldiers who were registered as such. Like my father. There may have been many more like that. But you can't say that they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to establish the facts. So do you really believe that there couldn't have been more than 3.000 men with weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. But on paper there were more, you say. You can't see that on the spot, as the column is moving, who is a soldier on paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: After the demilitarisation of the area, they may have still been recorded as soldiers, but they weren't really soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to the best of your knowledge, there were not more than 3.000 armed men in that column.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Maybe even fewer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that on that occasion a large number of people were killed, there was a lot of panic, let us just have a look at the first statement of the 19th of July when you describe what happened after that. You say that, "In the woods where I was with the others, I stayed for one day and one night. Throughout that time, the Chetniks kept shelling the place with Pragas, self-propelled anti-aircraft guns and anti-aircraft machine-guns and other weapons. That day people started arguing and killing each other. Some wanted to surrender and others did not." Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I have to add something. So this column, this army, they were maybe ten or 15 kilometres in front of us. So we remained there, surrounded. I assume we were surrounded. We didn't dare go anywhere. And the soldiers were calling out over the loudspeaker for us to surrender. Before that, there was shelling all the time. There were many people there. And when they started calling and telling us to surrender on the loudspeaker, and they said, "You will be escorted in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. If you don't surrender, you will be killed." The shelling had stopped then. And some people didn't wouldn't to go. Actually, some were in -- actually, it was just chaos. There were a lot of people wounded. People were dying. People were hallucinating. You could see men going crazy. They were yelling at night and -- this was a consequence of the conflict. When the Serbs were calling on us to surrender, the people who didn't want to would kill themselves. There weren't that many who did that, we didn't all go and kill ourselves. A few. I saw two or three cases of suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say they started quarreling amongst themselves and killing each other. So they were clashing -- clashes amongst them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes. They started arguing, but not killing each other, I meant killing themselves. I don't know in which statement I said this. I didn't see anyone killing someone else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm examining you only on the basis of the written statements received from the other side, and you say at the beginning of the second page of the statement I'm quoting from: "In the woods I was in with the other men, I stayed for one day and one night, and throughout that time the Chetniks were shelling the place with Pragas, PAMs, and other weapons. That day, people started arguing amongst themselves and killing each other. Some wanted to surrender and others did not. At one point a column headed towards the village of Sandici, and my cousin and I joined that column." That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: So what are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement, you say that, "In Kamenica, a large number of people were killed and many were wounded by shells. A certain number of our men committed suicide." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: It is true, but let me add something. So a part of the people decided to surrender. We were in the woods. We didn't know where we were, in fact. We were lost. And the previous day and all night until morning, there was shelling. There was fighting and shooting. That morning, it was quiet, and we were treading over the dead, the wounded. And when they started calling out, people didn't want to surrender until about 3.00. Those who did decide, they joined this column. Others who didn't, some fled. I saw one or two, three cases of people killing themselves. That's as many as I saw. But this is negligible compared to the number killed. There were far more wounded people. So many stayed behind in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but there was also a clash amongst the people there themselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Will you tell me where exactly I say that they were killing each other. Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is in the first statement, on page 2. At the top of the page, in the fourth line, you say exactly, and I'm quoting you: "They started arguing and killing each other or amongst themselves." It is at the beginning of the second page. You say: "They started arguing amongst themselves and killing each other."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: They started quarreling, yes, but they didn't kill each other. It may have happened if that had gone on, but I didn't see anyone kill anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just telling you what it says here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I understand what I'm reading. You're trying to persuade me that I said one thing, but this sentence is rather ambiguous, and it can be interpreted in two different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the army had gone forward, in front, and that the people who stayed in the woods were those who had joined the army. And if they were shooting, they must have been armed. Did you have any weapons there among the part of the column that you say consisted of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I told you, the army had almost passed through, and when the column was cut in half, virtually all the civilians stayed behind and maybe a small part of the army. I didn't see Serb soldiers. They were shelling so hard that -- harder than any time before. Maybe in 1993, at the beginning of the war. So the army had almost passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what you considered to be the whole army, though the whole column was virtually, consisted of able-bodied men following that order and there were a few of you who still had weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Maybe that is how it had been planned, that everyone should go, but army was up front, and they left first. So one could say that we were disappointed. We stayed behind them. And when the Serb army cut the column in two, those who remained were virtually all civilians. So most of the soldiers had passed through, but maybe a few were left behind. Maybe a part of the army stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now about those who remained after the main body of the army left. How many among those who remained were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps I happened to see someone with weapons but they did not surrender later. They fled. I saw people who didn't want to surrender, who simply fled. They didn't want to go and surrender. They simply went in a different direction, through the woods or something. And perhaps some of them who stayed behind did not surrender either. Not everybody wanted to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I see that in the statement you gave to the investigators you make no mention of these incidents of interfighting, interkilling among the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you mention this to the investigators at all or did they simply decide to leave it out? I assume that you told them the same things that you said in the first two statements.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I gave this statement or, rather, these two statements that you insist upon immediately after my survival, and I gave these statements to the investigators much later. So perhaps I did not remember all the details, but you keep insisting on them killing each other, killing each other, and you keep insisting on it. It is ambiguous. I mean, I meant that they were committing suicide. People were killing themselves in that sense, but your way of putting it is that we were killing each other in the sense of some people killing other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that a lot of people got killed during the fighting during the breakthrough, that a large number got killed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think you've exhausted this topic. You've been over and over it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add one more thing, just one more thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, we cannot call this a breakthrough. When the Serb army severed that column, most of them were civilians. I recognised so many neighbours. So it cannot be called a breakthrough when they cut through this column, then they surrounded the civilians. Perhaps there was a soldier or two there from that column that they had broken up, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1401, they could not have known whether you were civilians or not. You were part of this column that was fighting them; is that right? How could they know from a distance whether you were, because you were a part of the column consisting of able-bodied men, and you were asked to surrender in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, so they considered you to be the military.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, later on, too. You can understand this any way you want. I don't know what they considered us to be, but they planned to kill us, to kill all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What they were planning then will certainly have to be established, but tell me, please -- actually, just one more thing quite specific. Did this happen on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Can I just add one more thing? Well, while the army was passing there, there was no conflict. It could be seen very well. There are meadows after the forest, and you can see very well whether it's military or civilians. The Serbs did not kill those who had went ahead -- who had gone ahead. Only when the remainder came, that's when they cut through the column and started killing people. But the army had already passed ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, are you trying to say that they allowed the army to pass without fighting and then they started shooting and killing you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, there would have been a conflict in that case, and then some of them would have gotten killed too. So that's what I saw and that's what I infer on the basis of what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was this on the 12th of July? I'm asking you this because of some other witnesses who testified here. I just want to establish the date. Was this on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: On the 11th we set out, and we spent the night in the forest, and the next day was the 12th when they called --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you spent a day and night in that forest, on the following day, that is to say on the 13th of July, is that right, together with 600 other members of that group of yours on the road between Kasaba and Bratunac, you surrendered to the Serb forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say in your first statement: "As we were getting out to the asphalt road linking Kasaba and Bratunac, the Chetniks placed a tank there, a transporter, and we all came down onto the asphalt with our hands up. At that point the Chetniks took all our belongings; money, guns, and other valuables." Is that right? That's what is written here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement, you say: "After a day and night spent in the forest, we went to the asphalt road where the bridge we saw Chetniks with tanks and APCs who ordered us to raise our hands and drop the grenades, pistols, and German marks we had or we would be killed. We all obeyed their order." So when they issued the order, you surrendered your weapons. That means that you did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it looks when -- if the soldiers were saying it, but they were saying that the soldier -- the soldiers were saying that people who had weapons should surrender them, or those who had knives or razors or something. But nobody had a weapon. I don't remember seeing anyone with a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To hand over weapons that you did not have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You came across them, they asked you to surrender and to lay your weapons down, but you claim that you had no weapons; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: The same thing happened in my village in 1992. People surrendered their weapons and yet again they were asking for weapons. They just kept asking for weapons without any reason for doing so. Perhaps they were afraid that somebody had a pistol in their jackets or in their bags or something like that. That's what they were afraid of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so that's what they were afraid of. They could not see whether you had any weapons or not. Wasn't it visible? It was in broad daylight. They say surrender your weapons, and don't they see that you don't have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: They said that we should leave all our things, whoever had money. "Don't you let us find a razor on any one of you." Perhaps they thought that somebody had a pistol in the pockets of their coats or something but I didn't see anybody with a rifle or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not insisting on you saying something that you said you did not see. So tell me now, do you know that in the ranks of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in that area, there was a considerable number of persons who were underage who had been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Just one more thing that I wish to add in response to the other question, then I'm going to answer this question. I already told you that some soldiers in the forest who had rifles simply left. They didn't even surrender. Perhaps there was a soldier or two or something like that. But I didn't see anybody like that with me. There was no one like that where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, do you know how many minors were mobilised into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I don't know about the number of minors or whether there were any minors. Perhaps there were, perhaps there weren't, but I don't know. Let me just add one more thing. Actually, nobody was forced to go into the army because people did not have any weapons. I mean, even people who were of age and who were able-bodied did not have weapons. People would have liked to have been in the army perhaps. Perhaps I would have liked to have been in the army too because that would have given me greater chance of survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to go through all of this as fast I can, all of these questions. Please, tell me, since we stated at the beginning that 15.000 of you set out after the line-up, then this conflict occurred, the army broke through and part of you stayed behind. During this breakthrough, how many people actually got killed? What is your estimate? Out of the 15.000 of you who had set out, how many people got killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Not everybody was killed there. I didn't see all the persons who were killed, so this is a very approximate estimate. Perhaps I saw about 500 men. One person was lying by a beech tree, and then one person was without a face, and -- well, say about 500. I don't know. I mean, I didn't look through the entire forest. I was only in part of the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in the part of the forest that you saw, during that breakthrough, about 500 men were killed, or perhaps more. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that pertains to the part of the forest that you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes. Because I know that I was walking across bodies. There were so many people killed, and then also they were victims of shells, because you would see people without faces, hands, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the soldiers who took you prisoner then introduced themselves and they said that they were from Serbia. Is that what you're saying? That was my understanding --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- on the basis of the summary. So they introduced themselves to you and said they were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, when we were lined up down there, where they lined us up there and when they took our things away. Then we ran for about two or three kilometres, I don't know exactly, with our hands up. And then we came to a meadow where there was a tank where there were a lot of soldiers. I mean, I wasn't the first one to get there, there were others who had already arrived, and there were probably people there on the meadow even beforehand, and there was a burned Muslim village there that had been burned, I don't know when, before that. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: We came to the meadow and a soldier stood there in front, and I heard this very well. He had something on his head, and he said, "We are from Serbia." He was really full of himself. It's not only that. He started lecturing us there. He was acting really smart. I remembered some of this, but usually I did not listen, and I was with my head down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, 1401. I heard just now when your summary was read that these soldiers made you shout Long live the King and things like that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: When this soldier gave this lecture -- or, rather, the wounded were there in front, perhaps I was smaller so I couldn't see them very well, but later on when I was boarding the truck I did not see them. He said, "You see these comrades of yours? You should have surrendered earlier. You're going to be exchanged when your authorities ask for you. You're going to the hangar in Bratunac now." And then he said, mockingly, "You're not getting any dinner." It seemed ridiculous. There were so many of our men who were killed there, we were all terrified, and he's saying you're not getting any dinner. But he was laughing probably because he knew what lay in store for us. And when we lay there on the ground with our abdomens on the ground and we had to shout "Long live the King" and it resounded through the valley and our hands were up -- I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to give me the entire description now but isn't it clear to you these could not have been soldiers from Serbia who were forcing you to shout "Long live the King"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that they are from Serbia or that they're not from Serbia, but the fact is -- the fact is that the soldiers said that. And the fact is that we shouted that while they were probably killing the wounded, because later on I saw a soldier shooting at the house. And my uncle who was there said that a man was missing, a man who they probably took away. So they probably killed the wounded over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you just confirmed this, that these soldiers that you thought were from Serbia, they told you to shout "Long live the King."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I didn't think anything. The soldiers said, "We are from Serbia." I'm not saying anything what I think; I heard this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he said that and then he forced you to shout "Long live the King." Now tell me, please, from Kamenica you were transferred by trucks, as you said in your statements given to the investigators, you were transferred to Bratunac, and you spent the night there, one night, on trucks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On trucks where it said Tuzlatrans. That's what was written on the trucks. So it couldn't have been anybody from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Oh, just a moment, please. That's not what was written on all the trucks. On one of the trucks it said Tuzlatrans. It's not to say that the trucks were from Tuzla and that we were going to Tuzla. It probably belonged to a company. It just happened to be there. It happened to be in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then from Bratunac they transferred you by trucks again to a place where, as you said in your statement given to the investigators, that you did not know where this place was, but you do know that this was a school. That's what you said in your statement given to the investigators: "They transferred us somewhere but we did not know where." However, in your first statement, dated the 31st of July 1995, you say, "On the following day they drove us in trucks towards Konjevic Polje and then to Zvornik and Karakaj. And after that they allegedly went to Tuzla. Underneath the tarpaulin I saw that they took us to a school in Petkovci." So that is a quotation from your second statement. Please, explain this to me now: How is it possible that in your previous statement you said that as you were looking through the tarpaulin you managed to notice that you were in front of the school in Petkovci whereas in your statement that you gave later to the investigators you said that you did not know where they took you to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'll explain. Actually, we didn't know where they were taking us and I did not know it was a school when we were in front of the school, but later, when I entered the school, I saw it was a school. Later on, when I was taken into the school, I saw blackboards where children write and I saw the kind of floor you have in a school, and desks. It looked like a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you the following: You saw this later, and in the statement given to the organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 31st of July 1995, you said that they brought you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it really matter? Does it really matter when he found out it was a school? It's not disputed apparently that it was a school.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the point. The point is, Mr. May, that in the statement given to the investigators later, much later, he says - this is on page 7, paragraphs 1 through 5 - that he was not in a position to say where the school was. And in the previous statement, he already knew that this was the school in Petkovci, according to what the witness himself is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which statement? In which statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... let the witness clarify the point. You can deal with it without looking at the statement, Mr. Witness. Just tell us, when did you find out it was a school, and when did you find out it was in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After we entered the school. Before that, we did not know that it was a school, but after we got into the school, we saw blackboards, and there was even writing on the blackboards. And perhaps I heard it from the people there too. There were things written on the blackboards. Perhaps I didn't notice all of it, but afterwards, after entering the school, I realised that it was a school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're going to adjourn in a minute, but let's clarify this. When did you find out that it was in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know whether that is what is written here, that I found out that very moment, but I've remembered just now. After we escaped, when we reached the free territory, people were saying where we were as we were going through these villages. They were saying, aha, it could be this or it could be that. But then when we entered this place, we knew it was a school. So I remember that we were talking to people and they said, aha, that could be it, that could be Petkovci. And afterwards, I went there with the investigators, so I confirmed that that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now time to adjourn. And just -- we are going to adjourn now for 20 minutes, and Witness 1401, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. So don't speak to anybody, and that includes the Prosecution, during the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes. Perhaps I might draw the attention of the Prosecution to this, that we cannot sit beyond the usual time this afternoon. We have obviously some more cross-examination, ten minutes or so, of this witness. It's a question of whether you want to start the next witness or not. I doubt we'll finish him in the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an administrative matter to introduce some of the 92 bis packages for witnesses without cross. Maybe perhaps that's the best way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Nice has some matter he wishes to introduce too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be better to deal with that, and if we finish early, I don't think there will be any complaint. Yes, we will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to complete my examination in those ten minutes, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clear up this, Mr. 1401. I'm going to read out this sentence from your statement, because the point here is not the school itself but Petkovci. That is the point of my question. You say in your statement, and this is the one given on the 31st of July, on page 2: "I saw under the canvas that they had brought us to a school in Petkovci." So under the canvas you managed to see that they had brought you to a school in Petkovci. And in your statement to the investigators, you're unable to identify that school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he's explained that this was information which he got later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the school in Petkovci is mentioned in the statement given on the 31st of July, and the statement to the investigators was 12 days later. So in the statement he made on the 31st of July, he says, and I've quoted accurately, that he saw that they had been brought in front of the school in Petkovci, and 12 days later he doesn't know where they were brought to. So what you say would be quite logical if the events were in opposite sequence, but this statement given to the investigators was 12 days later in which he doesn't know where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can you explain that, Witness 1401?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I can. Once we had reached free territory, that is before I gave this statement, any statement, people were talking about where we were. So I knew definitively that we had been in Petkovci on the basis of what people were saying. Later on, when I made that statement, maybe I didn't mention it because I wasn't something I knew, but it was information I got from others. And the person who survived with me, maybe he knew. I'm not quite sure, he may have known. We may have discussed it on the way, but it was such a long time ago, I'm not quite sure. And after all this, the statements came. So I may have said we were taken to a school, but people were saying that the school was in Petkovci. So maybe in one statement I didn't mention it, and in another I did. But the other person who survived knows much more about that school, and I spoke to him about it, but I can't remember all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't wish to bother you any further with those questions, though you said that under the canvas you saw that you were brought to a school in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take your statement from the 31st of July. The 12th line from the top, and I'm reading you the whole sentence from the full stop to the full stop. "I saw under the canvas that they had brought us to a school in Petkovci," full stop. That is what it says, 12th line from the top, page 2, in your statement of the 31st of July. Twelve days later, talking to the investigators, you don't know where you were taken. It says clearly Petkovci. "I saw under the canvas that we had been brought to the school in Petkovci."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Doesn't it say here to a school? It doesn't say which.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it says in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: But on the basis of other information. I couldn't go into all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. I think you've given us sufficient explanation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't a hundred per cent sure. I described to the investigators that it was a school and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope what you're saying is clear to anyone listening. Now, tell me, please, you reached that school, according to what you told the investigators, on the 14th of July. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the 15th of July, the next day, you survived the execution that you describe. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Actually, it was during the night. I'm not sure if it was the 14th or the 15th; it may or been before midnight or after midnight; it was during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This execution that you described was survived also --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't know if I may mention the name of that person. If not, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- I only have a few more questions for you. Do you know who carried out the execution that you managed to survive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I not sure who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to give us a description of any kind of the persons who executed you and the others, or who shot at you and the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I can't remember all the details. Probably it was the Bosnian Serb army, but I can't confirm that. I remember a detail in front of the school when they forced us off the trucks. When we were beaten up in front of the school, everyone had to stand and be beaten. And when the man in front of me was waiting for his turn to come to be beaten, to be beaten with rifle butts and so on, the soldier asked him, "Do you know me?" And he said as follows: "Of course I know, brother." And then the soldier said, "Who do you know?" He hit him with his rifle in his stomach and then they started stamping on him and beating him up, as if he wasn't supposed to know him. Then I heard that that man was from Zvornicka Kamenica and that he used to be a colleague of his sometime in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that on that occasion you heard that one of those men was called Jovo. Can you tell me, did you hear any other name or surname of a person who was there, anyone who was there? Because the only fact I managed to find was that you mentioned that you heard somebody being called Jovo. Can you remember any other name, first or last, of anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I cannot give you any name. I didn't know anyone. There were probably people who recognised the soldiers where the shooting took place. This happened during the night. You will never be able to understand the circumstances, the feeling one has when you're taken out to be executed. I just remember that one name. There may have been others mentioned, but I haven't remembered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to how many people were shot dead on that occasion, according to what you have told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: It is hard to make an estimate. I was crawling over the bodies during the night. It was night-time. And when we reached the canal and untied each other, it was only from the other hill that we saw the loader loading bodies onto a tractor. The one who survived with me knows better because I was in pain. I was wounded, I was suffering. And I know that there were many people, as there was a loader being used, and I think I pointed in another trial where this was, but it is difficult to tell how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you must have had some impression as to how many of you there were in the truck.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that there was just one truckload of people that were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I couldn't see from the school whether there was a truck in front of us. After us came a tractor or a truck, because you can't see during the night. You could just see the nights. And when they reached the spot, we heard them firing shots. We don't know whether they were killing people or doing something else, but not with the same intensity or frequency as when I was shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to establish some sort of a figure. Could you assist how many people were executed, to the best of your knowledge, on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: It is very hard to say. I know that most of the people from the school were killed. We could see that. I don't know how many classrooms there were full of men, but when they were taken out, they were probably all killed. Because you could hear when they said, "Ten people come out," then you heard bursts of fire. My classroom was the last. I don't know whether that was the last truck too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of you were there in that classroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: The classroom was full. Maybe as many as on the truck, maybe more, I don't know. I can't say. It was full. We were sitting on top of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You can't tell me that either. Now, tell me, when did you find out that this execution that you're testifying about was carried out at the location Brnjice Djulici? I apologise if I'm mispronouncing the names of those locations. I don't know whether my notes are correct. Brnjice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I knew earlier on. It's not far from Karakaj. I used to go to Glinica and I knew that there was a dam there and some waterway, but I don't know what it looked like. And I assumed, I wasn't sure, but later on when we crossed into free territory and talking amongst ourselves, this man and woman that we saw, they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 1401, my question was when did you find out. So you learned that when you crossed into free territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: We didn't talk about that. Maybe this man who survived with me may have known before, but I assumed that, and later on I found out exactly. But this was before I made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you when did you find out what the location was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: When I crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you crossed over into free territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, tell me, please, did you know that before the investigators took you to that spot for you to identify it, or did you establish that when they took you there to the spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I assumed that that was it. People told me later on, "That is the dam near Karakaj, Djulici." And I later went with the investigators to confirm that that was the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that where the school in Petkovci is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Not that close by. Petkovci is another village. I didn't know about Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you were detained in the school in Petkovci and then taken out and executed -- so you were executed in front of the school in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: They took us by truck to the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. They took you in a truck from Petkovci to the dam. And you learnt about the spot when the investigators took you there to identify it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: You keep saying, and I am telling you, I knew -- I assumed that it was the dam there in Karakaj. Later, I learnt from others, once we had crossed, when we reached this village, when we said where we had been, when we described the spot, then they said what it was. I later just went to confirm it with the investigators, and I confirmed that that was the spot. It may have another name, I don't know what the name is, but I took them to that spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic. You've had well over ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood that you were wounded, because you explained that, but in your first statement, of the 15th of July, you said that you were wounded in the stomach area, and in your second statement in the chest, the lower arm of your right hand. Where exactly were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I was wounded on the right side - you can call it whatever you like - and in my right arm. You can call it the right side of my chest or whatever. So the investigators carried out detailed examinations and took all the documents and the X-rays. You can call it as you like. You can look at the X-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your first statement that you were wounded in the stomach. Afterwards, you said in the chest, and that is why I'm inquiring, because I only just received the binder with the photographs, which I haven't had time to look at, and that's why I asked you to explain for me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is really important, whether it was the stomach or the chest, but anyway it was my right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 1401.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May. I managed within the time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to make something clear. The statements that Mr. Milosevic showed the witness here were translated into English over here. In addition to those two statements and those that the witness gave to the investigators, and that is the only thing that I will be dealing with, there is yet another statement given to the investigative judge in Tuzla, and in this part of the world it was the investigative judges who were always the most professional of all in terms of conducting such investigations. 348/95 is the number that was assigned by that court of that document, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So do you remember, sir, that this statement that you gave on the 24th of July, 1995, to the investigative judge, is yet another statement that you gave, that you signed, and do you recall these things that you mentioned in that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I remembered that I gave a statement to judges, but I have forgotten the date, and I've forgotten the year even. So I signed it when I gave it. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: There seems to be something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You'll see it can be found. There are a few pages there, and now I'm going to show you a few things from that page that is in front of you. Tell me, is that what you said to the investigative judge then? "We heard that UNPROFOR from that elevation that it held then withdrew towards Srebrenica." Do you remember having stated that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: That's my statement. That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you move on to say that you went to the village of Viogor. You explained that, I won't take you back to all of that. But then you say there, "In that village, we heard that members of our army made the Chetniks go back to their initial positions, and then our people withdrew again, that is to say our forces had fallen back to their earlier positions." Is that to say that there were conflicts there too and that there were casualties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Let me just add a few more details. All of this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all of this is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Let me just add something. The place that we came to, it's ten or 15 kilometres away from where the fighting was going on. It's a hill, some heights that are very far away. But where we were, there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But what is stated here is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Could you please read this out to me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "There we first heard that members of our army had pushed the Chetniks back to their initial positions and soon after that they had retreated again, that is that our forces had fallen back to their earlier positions."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Oh, what we heard about the army, it did not pertain to us. It pertained to the Zeleni Jadar road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But there was fighting between the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who removed the Chetniks, as you had put it, from their positions and they took them again and then there was fighting there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then a few sentences later, you say: "In the morning we heard from the army that it was expected that NATO aeroplanes would bomb the Serb forces and tanks and that our forces were planning to execute a counter-attack if that happened in order to retake the lost positions." That means that you heard that from the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that that is what would happen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: I think the statement is brief, so that's why not only details were included. I gave the statement to the judges perhaps for two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tapuskovic please not overlap the witness. The interpreter could not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw that there were civilians there and we saw that there were military people there, so that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this is what you said and this is what you testified to here: "I saw that NATO aircraft were flying over and dropping bombs. But the bombs fell beside the tanks." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: It can be seen even if it is far away. I did not see the actual bombs, I saw the smoke from the areas where the bombs were actually falling and we saw the aeroplanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see the bombs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: How could I see the bombs? They were so far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear them, at least?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, explosions were heard and shells, so perhaps it was hard to distinguish between the two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you slow down so the interpreters have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said that you saw this here with your very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Well, I saw this smoke where it is most probable that the bombs fell, but I couldn't see the bombs themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look a bit further down. I'm not going to go back to what was already dealt with. And you say that in accordance with the order issued by the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were 15.000 men lined up there, and you said, "We crossed the Chetnik line" and then the name of the place is illegible. It says Buglic or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. And then you say: "From there --" or, rather, "It is there that we crossed the Chetnik lines." Is that where there was a breakthrough or what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: That's where the front line was, somewhere around there. But I already said earlier on that the Serb army did not even clash with the BH army because they had already left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here you said that you went across the line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: But there were trenches there. It's a fact that that's where the Chetnik line was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you arrived in the village of Kamenica, as you put it here, that belongs to the village of Pobudje in Bratunac municipality. "At the entrance to Kamenica we ran into a Chetnik ambush." Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: When there are so many people involved, when it's 5.000 or 2.000 people going, and when you hear gunfire, I mean, it wasn't that I was looking at all this from an aeroplane.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you put this very clearly. Could you just tell me whether it was the way you described it here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: But it's not marked here. I don't know where I said it. Which page is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's all on the first page. All of this is on the first page, towards the end. You mentioned the number of people who were in that column, and then you say, we crossed the Chetnik column at such-and-such a place and then we were ambushed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: It's a short statement. So not all details were mentioned. I gave a statement to The Hague investigators for two days whereas I spoke to these judges for two hours. So I don't see what you don't find very clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything. I'm saying that it's all very clear to me. I just thought that you should tell the Trial Chamber whether this is what happened, and if so, tell us, please, it says here that you saw 300 to 500 persons who had been killed. All of that happened before you were taken prisoner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Let me just say something. Well, it's a fact that the Serb lines were around Srebrenica. We did not have a highway. We could not have gone along a highway. So this is a fact. And what is in dispute? The Serb army had probably left when we crossed the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you give the figure involving the persons who were killed? They were killed before you were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave on the 12th and 13th of August, 1995, that is to say only a few days after this statement, so this is page 9, in response to the investigator's question, you said: "Later on I saw --" the last sentence. It's the last sentence on page 9. "Later on I saw that I had more -- several cuts on my neck and right hand. I don't know whether I was grazed by bullets or rocks."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And a few minutes ago when answering the Prosecutor's question, you said that you were hit in the left foot. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then two more times, in addition, to the left foot. That's what you said a few minutes ago when you were answering the Prosecutor's questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: May I explain? All this happened during the night, and it was probably fragmentation bullets that were used, and I still have, on the right side and in my right foot and in my right arm, some leftover pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Witness, could you please explain to the Judges something which is difficult to explain in any other way but one, because in this statement you gave to the investigative judge, the one that you looked at a few minutes ago, please look at page 3 towards the end: "I was wounded by Chetnik gunfire coming from an automatic rifle, in the lower right arm and in the right side of the chest." How is it possible for one and the same thing to be described in different ways, especially wounds that you can show people? How can you explain that in so many different ways? Could you just explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1401
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Well, you expect me to say the very same thing in every statement, the very same sentence, but it's just worded a bit differently. So I was hit by this fragmentation ammunition. I assume that that's what it was. Later on, the investigators saw the X-rays, too, and -- but there was this burst of gunfire, yes, I know that. Fragmentation bullets too. After the X-rays were taken, I realised that it was fragmentation ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
